title: Padres set franchise record for worst loss, fall 23-3 to Cubs
content:
With the wind blowing out Wednesday at Wrigley Field, the San Diego Padres matched a franchise worst and established two others in a 23-3 rout by the Chicago Cubs.

That matched the most runs the Padres have ever allowed, equaling the total on May 17, 1977, in another embarrassing loss at Wrigley Field. The Cubs’ eight home runs — three off starter Walker Buehler, three off reliever Kyle Hart and two off catcher Rodolfo Duran — were the most they have ever surrendered. The margin of defeat was the largest in San Diego history.

“It’s going as poorly as it can right now,” manager Craig Stammen told reporters after the Padres’ losing streak reached five games. “We got to find a way to dig deep, dig our way out of that hole. I think there’s some grit on this team and we got to dig deep for that. … If we get negative, we turn on each other, we start pointing fingers, that’s when it’ll turn into disaster.”

As Stammen attempted to preserve a taxed bullpen amid a blowout, Buehler was charged with a career-high nine runs over four innings. Since May 19, San Diego’s patchwork rotation has produced a 5.22 ERA and only four quality starts. The Padres are 14-24 in that span, evoking memories of their second-half collapse in 2021, when they essentially ran out of big-league-caliber starting pitching.

Chicago’s eight home runs tied a Cubs team record set nearly a year ago, on July 4, 2025, at Wrigley Field against the St. Louis Cardinals. The 23 runs scored was the most for the Cubs since they tied a franchise record with 26 at Colorado on August 18, 1995.

Cubs manager Craig Counsell has pointed out that Wrigley Field is as unique a ballpark as there is in the game. During the colder months, the wind blows in from Lake Michigan and suppresses offense. Position players can get frustrated as well-struck balls get knocked down by a punishing gust. But the Padres came into town just as summer arrived. The temperatures were above 90 degrees for all three games with a strong wind blowing out.

“The conditions the last three days are so unique,” Counsell said. “There’s no place that ever plays like this, not even close.”

The Cubs took full advantage, especially over the last two games, when they combined to hit 13 home runs. Dansby Swanson slugged five of those homers, including three on Wednesday.  Over his last 10 games, Swanson has driven in 26 runs — eight came on Wednesday — to put him in elusive company.

This all comes not long after Swanson was so cold that his manager had dropped him to ninth in the batting order and fans and members of the media began to wonder if an extended benching was needed for the veteran. In his first 70 games of the season, Swanson hit .175 with seven home runs and 28 RBIs. Over his last 13 games, Swanson has raised his batting average 35 points, slugged nine homers and driven in 29 runs.

“We never have baseball figured out,” Counsell said. “I think this tells you that. He probably went through the roughest patch of his career. On the other side of it is the best stretch of his career. You figure it out.”

Entering Wednesday, Buehler had delivered a 2.64 ERA over his previous nine starts. The Cubs slugged three home runs off him, with Seiya Suzuki getting it started with a three-run shot in the first and Swanson hitting one each in the second and third against Buehler.

“We made it really hard on him and he never got comfortable,” Counsell said. “In the end, that’s the game. We did a lot of stuff late, but what we did against Buehler is what kind of determines the outcome of the game. We did a great job against a pitcher that’s been throwing the ball well.”

For the first time since 2017, the Padres have allowed at least 15 runs multiple times in a five-game span. San Diego lost 15-3 to the Los Angeles Dodgers on Saturday, when Randy Vásquez — pitching after an opener — allowed seven runs in 3 1/3 innings (and Duran made his professional pitching debut). On Thursday, Vásquez is slated to be lined up to face the Dodgers again, this time in the opener of a four-game series.

“It only counts as one (loss), and we got to remember that,” Stammen said. “Unfortunately, it’s in a stretch of some tough games and, for us, some tough losses.”
